design_detail: Open before-and-after pharmacokinetic study in 8 men who had used amphetamines recreationally. An oral challenge dose of deuterated S-(+)-methamphetamine was given on day 1, followed by 13 days of 10 mg a day of a slow-release oral preparation of S-methamphetamine taken each morning in the laboratory, and the same challenge dose again on day 15. Two challenge dose levels were studied in separate rounds about three months apart, 0.125 and 0.250 mg/kg, with six men at each level and four taking part in both. Plasma was sampled to 48 hours, saliva to 24 hours and urine to 72 hours; concentrations of the deuterated challenge drug, the non-deuterated daily drug and their amphetamine metabolites were measured separately by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. A one-compartment model with first-order absorption and a lag time was fitted to each person's plasma curve, and day-15 parameters were subtracted from day-1 parameters within person.
can_establish: Whether the absorption, distribution, clearance, half-life and urinary excretion of a fixed oral dose of methamphetamine change after thirteen days of daily low-dose exposure, within the same men, and how large a change the study could have detected.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance develops to any effect of methamphetamine: subjective and cardiovascular measures were taken but are reported in the companion paper, not here. It also cannot establish anything about other routes, larger doses or binge patterns, or about women, who were not studied.

sample.recruitment: Paid, informed male volunteers familiar with the recreational use of amphetamines; the recruitment route is not described (p. 857).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 19-32 in good health by medical and psychiatric history and physical examination, eating a normal diet, not currently using tobacco, prescription or over-the-counter drugs; each contracted to abstain from the recreational use of amphetamines or any other drug for two weeks before the experiment and throughout it, with daily urine screening by EMIT for cannabis, opiates, amphetamines, phencyclidine, cocaine metabolite, barbiturates, methadone, propoxyphene, ethanol, benzodiazepines and methaqualone (p. 857).
sample.demographics: Eight men, weight 73.5 kg (SD 2.9), aged 19-32. No further demographic information is given; race, education and amphetamine-use history are not reported (p. 857).
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported, but several pharmacokinetic parameters are based on fewer than six people: the amount excreted in urine and the urinary rate constant rest on 3 or 4 of the 6 in each low-dose condition, because complete urine collection was not achieved for everyone (Table 1, p. 858).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy men, non-smokers, with recreational amphetamine experience but excluded if currently using any drug; a sample chosen for a clean pharmacokinetic measurement rather than for resembling people who use methamphetamine regularly.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory and measured directly: splitless gas chromatography with positive chemical-ionization mass spectrometry and selected-ion monitoring quantified deuterated and non-deuterated methamphetamine and amphetamine separately, using more highly deuterated internal standards; replicate analyses over 1-25 ng/mL varied by 1-7% for methamphetamine (pp. 857-858).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral challenge capsule of deuterated S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride at 0.125 or 0.250 mg/kg, swallowed with 50 mL of water, on day 1 and again on day 15; between them, 10 mg a day of a slow-release oral preparation (Desoxyn Gradumet) each morning for 13 days (p. 857).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were not currently using tobacco, prescription or over-the-counter drugs and contracted to abstain from all other drugs; daily urine screening showed no compliance problems (pp. 857-858).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks' abstinence before the study and throughout, with daily urine screening. The day-15 challenge was given on top of residual drug from the daily dosing: non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 6.08 ng/mL (SEM 0.94) and amphetamine 2.3 ng/mL (SEM 0.3) at the start of day 15 (pp. 857-858).

comparison.controls: The same men on day 1, before the daily dosing began; there was no placebo condition and no separate control group. The two challenge doses are also compared with each other by two-sample t test, since not everyone received both.
comparison.matching: Within-person before-and-after, with day-15 parameters subtracted from day-1 parameters for each person; the order is fixed by the design.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person pharmacokinetic comparison.

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental and one-compartment model-derived pharmacokinetic parameters: peak concentration, time to peak, the extrapolated concentration at time zero, absorption and elimination rate constants and half-lives, lag time, apparent total and renal clearance, amount excreted in urine, urinary excretion constant and the percentage of dose recovered in urine; plus saliva-to-plasma ratios. Subjective and cardiovascular measures were taken by the methods of the companion paper but are not reported here (pp. 857-858).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard pharmacokinetic methods with a validated stereoselective assay; the model choice (one compartment with lag time) is justified against a two-compartment fit.
outcomes.operationalization: Pharmacokinetic tolerance is operationalized as a significant within-person change in a model parameter between day 1 and day 15, and its absence is quantified by a power analysis giving the detectable difference for each parameter.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: thirteen parameters were each tested at two dose levels by a one-sample t test or a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with a Shapiro-Wilk test used to choose between them, and the dose contrast by a two-sample t test with Satterthwaite's approximation where variances differed (p. 858).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: an open study with no placebo condition. The assay itself is objective and the isotope label distinguishes the challenge dose from the daily dose.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 gives means with standard errors and the number contributing to each cell; Table 2 gives, for each parameter and dose, the day-1 mean with upper and lower detection limits, the observed day-15 difference as a percentage and the difference the study could have detected. The two significant changes are both at the larger challenge dose: the extrapolated zero-time concentration rose from 47.34 ng/mL (SEM 1.06) to 51.39 (SEM 0.91), about 8.5%, and the peak concentration from 37.2 ng/mL (SEM 1.3) to 41.8 (SEM 1.7), about 12.5%. Elimination half-life averaged 10.14 h (SEM 0.63) overall, with condition means of 8.46, 9.71, 11.45 and 10.93 h; the discussion gives 10.1 h (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h. The percentage of the dose excreted in urine was higher at the smaller dose than the larger (54.1% against 34.6% on day 1; 50.0% against 30.0% on day 15).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person differences and two-sample dose comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study was approved by the University of North Carolina committee for the protection of human subjects (p. 857).
analysis.selective_reporting: The subjective and cardiovascular measures collected in the same sessions are reported only in the companion paper; area under the curve appears in the power table but not in Table 1; the urine and saliva data are presented mostly as figures.
analysis.power: Unusually well handled for a study of this period: Table 2 gives, for every parameter at both doses, the difference that could have been detected with a two-sided test at 5% and 80% power. A 20% change in the elimination rate constant, peak concentration and area under the curve would have been detected (detectable differences 21.2% and 14.8%, 18.3% and 6.1%, 20.1% and 15.6%); for absorption rate, lag time, time to peak and the urinary measures the detectable differences are 29.7% to 156.5%, so those null results are uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Thirteen days of daily low-dose methamphetamine left absorption, apparent clearance, apparent metabolic clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and half-life statistically unchanged. The only significant changes were at the larger challenge dose, where the extrapolated zero-time concentration was about 8.5% higher and the peak concentration about 12.5% higher on day 15. Both changes raise, not lower, the concentration reached by a given dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that minor pharmacokinetic differences after subchronic treatment would act to increase plasma concentration, so that pharmacodynamic tolerance could not be explained by a change in pharmacokinetics; the conclusion repeats this for the heart-rate tolerance reported in the companion paper. This follows from the results for the parameters the study could test precisely, and the power table is printed so that a reader can see which null results are informative. The qualification the paper does not make in its abstract is that the tolerance it is explaining was measured in the same six men at only the smaller dose, in an open study, so the inference is only as strong as that finding.

timeline.event: The clinical arm of the same programme, in the six men of the low-dose round: a smaller heart-rate rise on day 15, with unchanged ratings of 'high'
Smoked and intravenous methamphetamine in 6 men: half-life 11.1-12.2 h, consistent with the 10.1 h found here for the oral route
Three days of twice-daily oral dosing with tolerance to positive subjective effects; no plasma concentrations were measured, so the pharmacokinetic question was not revisited

replication.where_it_stands: This remains the only human study of methamphetamine pharmacokinetics before and after a course of daily dosing. Its half-life estimate agrees with later studies by other routes, but the finding that daily dosing does not induce its own metabolism rests on this study alone, at one low daily dose.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse contract 271-87-8126 (p. 856).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Research Triangle Institute with the University of North Carolina Department of Psychiatry; this paper and Perez-Reyes et al. (1991) report different measures from one study in the same men, so they are not independent sources.

what_would_settle_it: A repeated-dosing study at doses and by routes closer to non-medical use, with plasma sampling long enough to measure accumulation, a placebo challenge arm, and the subjective and cardiovascular measures reported alongside the concentrations, so that the presence of tolerance and the absence of a pharmacokinetic explanation are established in the same analysis.

domains.domain: Randomization process (no randomization: fixed before-and-after order)
domains.note: Day 1 always preceded day 15, there was no placebo challenge, and the two dose rounds were run about three months apart rather than allocated.

domains.domain: Period and carryover effects (within-person before and after)
domains.note: The day-15 challenge was given on a background of steady-state drug (6.08 ng/mL, SEM 0.94) and metabolite, but the deuterium label separates the two sources analytically, and the isotopomers are shown to share the same terminal elimination rate.

Open study with no placebo, which matters little for an assay-based outcome but means nothing is blinded; daily dosing was supervised in the laboratory and urine screening showed no compliance problems.
Complete urine collection was achieved for only 3 or 4 of 6 men in several conditions, so the excretion parameters rest on subsets, and the half-life estimates come from all six.
A validated stereoselective assay with deuterated internal standards, replicate variation of 1-7% for methamphetamine, and model fits whose coefficients of variation are printed for each parameter.

No protocol, 26 uncorrected within-person tests, and area under the curve reported only in the power table; against this, the power analysis for every parameter is printed, which is the opposite of selective reporting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The measurement is the strongest part of this study: a stereoselective isotope-label assay, per-person model fits and a printed power analysis make the null results interpretable for the parameters that were measured precisely. The design, however, is an open before-and-after comparison in six men per dose with no placebo challenge, which is why the overall judgment stays at the level of its weakest domains. The source can be cited for the absence of a change in absorption, clearance and half-life after thirteen days of low daily dosing, for the small rise in peak concentration at the larger challenge dose, and for oral pharmacokinetic values; it cannot be cited for tolerance to any effect, which it did not measure.

key_findings.finding: After thirteen days of 10 mg a day, the pharmacokinetics of the same oral challenge dose were essentially unchanged: absorption, apparent clearance, apparent metabolic clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and the elimination half-life did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15 at either challenge dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859, right column, continuing p. 860); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 860, right column)

key_findings.finding: Two parameters did change, both at the larger challenge dose and both upward: the extrapolated zero-time concentration rose from 47.34 ng/mL (SEM 1.06) on day 1 to 51.39 (SEM 0.91) on day 15, about 8.5% higher, and the peak concentration from 37.2 ng/mL (SEM 1.3) to 41.8 (SEM 1.7), about 12.5% higher (p<=0.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, C1 and Cmax rows with footnotes b and c (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859)

key_findings.finding: The study states what it could have detected: Table 2 gives the detectable difference for each parameter at each dose with 80% power. A 20% change would have been detected in the elimination rate constant (detectable 21.2% at the smaller dose, 14.8% at the larger), peak concentration (18.3% and 6.1%) and area under the curve (20.1% and 15.6%), while for absorption rate, lag time and the urinary measures the detectable differences run from 29.7% to 156.5%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Observed Difference and Detectable Difference columns

key_findings.finding: The elimination half-life of oral S-(+)-methamphetamine averaged 10.14 h (SEM 0.63, n=24 profiles), with condition means of 8.46, 9.71, 11.45 and 10.93 h; the discussion gives 10.1 h (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h. Peak concentrations were reached about 3 hours after dosing (overall time to peak 3.13 h, SEM 0.24) after a lag of about half an hour.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, elimination t1/2, tmax and Lag time rows (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 859); Conclusion (p. 862)

key_findings.finding: Daily dosing produced measurable steady-state concentrations: at the start of day 15, before the challenge, non-deuterated methamphetamine from the daily slow-release dose averaged 6.08 ng/mL (SEM 0.94) and its amphetamine metabolite 2.3 ng/mL (SEM 0.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > Concentrations in Biological Fluids, 1st paragraph (p. 857, right column, continuing p. 858)

key_findings.finding: Renal excretion was large and dose-dependent: 54.1% of the smaller dose against 34.6% of the larger was recovered in urine on day 1 (50.0% against 30.0% on day 15), and renal clearance depended on urine pH (p=0.0001), urine flow (p=0.0001) and dose (p=0.0003). Average renal clearance, 164 mL/min, exceeded the usual glomerular filtration rate of about 125 mL/min, which the authors read as active secretion.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, % dose in urine row (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 1st paragraph of p. 860; Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 860, right column)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine, the metabolite, reached much lower concentrations than the parent drug and peaked much later: 1.6 ng/mL (SEM 0.2) after the smaller dose and 4.0 (SEM 0.5) after the larger, at 11.7 h (SEM 0.8) against about 3.1 h for methamphetamine, with an area under the curve about 30% of the parent drug's; 15.1% (SEM 2.0) of the methamphetamine dose was recovered in urine as amphetamine on a molar basis.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 2nd-4th paragraphs of p. 860 (left column)

key_findings.finding: Saliva concentrations averaged 7.76 times (SEM 0.51, 149 paired samples) those in plasma, but the relationship was loose: linear regression gave r-squared 0.498 (p<0.0001), improved only to 0.620 by adding saliva pH and the logarithms of both measures, so saliva cannot be used to predict a plasma concentration accurately.
key_findings.locator: Results > Concentrations in Biological Fluids, 2nd paragraph (p. 858); Figure 3 (p. 859); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 861)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the area under the curve for the smaller challenge dose on day 1 is 312 ng.hr/mL and for the larger 735, while the Discussion gives 330 and 755 for the same parameter. Neither figure appears in Table 1, which does not list area under the curve at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two sets of values circulate for the same quantity; the Discussion figures appear to average the day-1 and day-15 values, so the day-specific figures in Table 2 are the ones to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the maximum concentrations of the challenge drug as 20.0 and 39.5 ng/mL 'table 1', but Table 1 prints 19.8 (SEM 2.7) and 20.3 (SEM 3.0) for the smaller dose on days 1 and 15 and 37.2 (SEM 1.3) and 41.8 (SEM 1.7) for the larger.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quoted pair are averages of the two study days, not table entries; a reader checking them against Table 1 will not find them, and the day-15 value for the larger dose is one of the study's two significant findings, which the averaging hides.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that quantities of the challenge drug averaging 30-54% of the dose were excreted in urine 'together with lesser amounts of S-methamphetamine-d3 (10-23% of dose)'; the second compound must be the metabolite S-amphetamine-d3, as the following sentences and Figures 4 and 5 make clear.
reporting_issues.consequence: As printed, the sentence says the same compound was excreted in two different amounts; the 10-23% figure belongs to amphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that a difference of 20% in the elimination rate constant, peak concentration and area under the curve could have been detected, but Table 2 gives detectable differences of 21.2% for the elimination rate constant and 20.1% for the area under the curve at the smaller dose, both just above 20%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim is right for the larger dose and marginally wrong for the smaller; the per-parameter values in Table 2 should be cited rather than the rounded statement.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 cells rest on fewer participants than the others (amount excreted in urine and the urinary rate constant on 3 or 4 of 6; renal clearance on 3, 6, 6 and 4), and the table does not say why; the reason, incomplete urine collection, appears only in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The urinary parameters are less precise than the plasma ones, and their dose comparison rests on small subsets.

reporting_issues.issue: The elimination half-life is given three ways: 10.1 hr in the abstract, an overall mean of 10.14 h (SEM 0.63) in Table 1, and 10.1 (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h in the conclusion; the Results also note that computing the half-life from the mean rate constant instead would give 9.32 h.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error, but a reader should cite the table value with its standard error and note which averaging method was used.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 856-862 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/Cook_1992_PKRepeatedDailyDosing.pdf). The embedded text layer is scrambled in reading order, so the pages were rendered at 300 dpi and read with optical character recognition; Table 1 (p. 858) and Table 2 (p. 861) were then checked cell by cell against the page images.
